Payments, mandates and reconciliation

After this lesson you can:
  • Describe the collection rails: NACH, UPI AutoPay, and their mandate lifecycles
  • Walk the bounce-and-retry flow with its charges and notices
  • Explain three-way reconciliation and the break queue

Learning rhythm: read one section at a time, pause to explain the control in your own words, then answer the knowledge check without looking back.

On this page
  1. The rails that pull EMIs
  2. When the debit bounces
  3. Reconciliation: trust, then verify
  4. Regulatory anchors
  5. Where this lives in LoanOS
  6. Knowledge check

1. The rails that pull EMIs

Repayment at scale is mandate-based: NACH (the bank-account auto-debit rail — mandate registered, amended, suspended or cancelled with the bank) and UPI AutoPay (UPI-based recurring debit), plus standing instructions and plain transfers. The mandate has its own lifecycle a BA must model: setup with borrower authentication, amendment on EMI change, suspension during disputes, cancellation at closure.

Remember the fund-flow rule from module 4: repayments flow directly from borrower to RE — collection into LSP wallets is prohibited, with narrow permitted exceptions. Cash collection in the field exists (module 6) under same-day posting and receipt controls.

2. When the debit bounces

A mandate presentation can return unpaid — insufficient funds, closed account, mandate cancelled. The return arrives with a reason code that drives everything after it:

  1. Post the bounce with its reason; the instalment is now overdue and DPD starts counting.
  2. Levy the bounce charge only if the KFS disclosed it — and as a charge, never capitalising penal interest.
  3. Notify the borrower and schedule the retry per policy.
  4. Repeated technical failures (mandate defects) route to a repair workflow, not to the borrower's conduct record.

Section 138 (cheque dishonour) becomes relevant when instrument-based repayment bounces — a recovery lever module 6 covers.

3. Reconciliation: trust, then verify

Every day, three views must agree: what the provider says happened, what the bank statement shows, what the ledger posted.

Three-way reconciliation matches them; mismatches enter a break queue with ageing, investigation, approval and (rarely) write-off.

Unidentified receipts sit in suspense until owned.

Duplicate protection is structural — idempotent ingestion means a replayed settlement file cannot double-post.

A BA designing any payment feature must answer: how does this reconcile, what breaks can it create, and who clears them?

Regulatory anchors

  • RBI-FUND-FLOW — Repayments flow directly to the RE; no LSP-controlled collection accounts.
  • RBI-PAY-DATA — Payment-system data stays in India; masking/tokenisation for stored artefacts.
  • RBI-FPC-PENAL — Bounce charges are disclosed charges, never capitalised penal interest.

Family IDs resolve in the India regulatory register (docs/compliance/india-regulatory-register.md), which owns sources and caveats.

Where this lives in LoanOS

  • Capability PAY-001 — NACH mandate setup, amendment, suspension and cancellation.
  • Capability PAY-005 — Bounce/return reason, charge, retry and borrower notice.
  • Capability PAY-013 — Daily provider-to-bank-to-ledger reconciliation.
  • Capability PAY-011 — Duplicate-payment protection and idempotency.

Retrieval practice

Knowledge check

Answer aloud or write your choice before opening the explanation. If you miss it, revisit the named section—not the whole lesson.

1. A settlement file is accidentally ingested twice. What protects the borrower's account?

  1. Manual review catches it monthly
  2. Idempotent ingestion — the duplicate posting is rejected structurally
  3. The bank refunds
  4. Nothing; reversals are raised later
Reveal answer and reasoning

B. Financial-event ingestion is idempotent by design; duplicate protection is a ledger property, not an ops process.

2. An EMI bounces with 'insufficient funds'. Which action is NOT allowed?

  1. Posting the overdue and starting DPD
  2. Levying the KFS-disclosed bounce charge
  3. Adding the charge to principal so interest accrues on it
  4. Notifying the borrower and retrying per policy
Reveal answer and reasoning

C. Capitalising charges is prohibited — penal/bounce charges are flat charges, never added to the interest-bearing principal.
